title: Heaps and RID Lookups
description: On a heap, a nonclustered seek does a RID Lookup per row; a covering index eliminates the lookup.
narrative:
## Scenario
`Orders` is a **heap** — a table with *no clustered index*. A screen runs `SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total, Status FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 42`. There is a nonclustered index on `CustomerId`, yet the query still does far more I/O than the ~40 rows it returns.

## Why it's slow
A heap stores rows in no particular order and identifies each by a physical **RID** (file:page:slot). The nonclustered index on `CustomerId` can **seek** to the matching index rows, but it only holds `CustomerId` (plus the RID). To fetch `OrderDate`, `Total`, and `Status` the engine must follow each RID back into the heap — a **RID Lookup**, driven by a **Nested Loops** operator, once per matching row.

## What to look for
- In the plan: an **Index Seek** feeding a **Nested Loops** that does a **RID Lookup** into `Orders`.
- In `STATISTICS IO`: logical reads well above the row count — one lookup per row.

## The concept
This is the heap version of a Key Lookup. Eliminate it the same way: make the index **covering** with `INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total, Status)` so the seek returns every needed column and never touches the heap. (Adding a clustered index is the other common fix — it changes lookups from RID Lookups to Key Lookups, but covering the query removes the lookup entirely.)
startingQuery: SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total, Status FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 42;
hints: The seek finds the rows, but which operator fetches the other columns? Look for a Nested Loops / RID Lookup on Orders.
IX_Orders_CustomerId holds only CustomerId — it can't supply OrderDate, Total, or Status without a lookup into the heap.
Create a covering index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Cust_Cov ON dbo.Orders(CustomerId) INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total, Status);
